lesson.title: Base rates and Bayes

steps.headline: Natural frequencies turn percentages into counts of people, which makes a test result easy to read.

lead.text: Picture 1,000 people. If 2% have a condition, that is 20 people. If a test catches half of them, that is 10 true positives. Counting people avoids multiplying percentages in your head.
A percentage of a group is a number of people. Work with the number.
1,000 people are screened for a disease that 1% have. The test flags 90% of those who have it, so there are 9 true positives. It also wrongly flags 10% of people who do not have the disease.

reveal.text: False positives outnumber the true positives by more than ten to one. The healthy group is large, so even a small error rate flags many people.

steps.headline: The chance that a positive result is right is the true positives divided by all positives.

lead.text: A positive result puts you among everyone the test flagged: the true positives plus the false positives. Most people answer near the test's hit rate instead. Ignoring how rare the condition is, is base-rate neglect.
Ask who is in the flagged group, and how many of them have the condition.

steps.headline: 500 people are tested; 10% have the disease. The test flags 60% of cases and 20% of healthy people. What share of positives are right?

workedSteps.text: Split the people into those with and without the disease.
Count the true positives and the false positives.
Divide the true positives by all positives.

reveal.text: Only 9 of the 108 flagged people have the disease. Answering with the test's 90% hit rate would be badly wrong.

lead.text: Of 1,000 people, 9 true positives and 99 false positives test positive. A person is among the flagged.
Use the same test, with a 90% hit rate and a 10% false-alarm rate, in a clinic where 10% of 1,000 people have the disease.

reveal.text: Nothing about the test changed, yet a positive now means far more. The meaning of a result depends on who is being tested.

lead.text: In a city, 20% of cabs are blue and the rest green. A witness names colours correctly 75% of the time. Picture 1,000 cabs: 200 blue and 800 green.

reveal.text: A witness who names colours reliably is still more likely wrong than right here, because green cabs are so much more common.

lesson.orientation: Turn a test result into a probability by counting people, so the base rate cannot be ignored.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: At an airport, 1,000 bags are scanned and 2 of them hold a banned item. The scanner beeps for both of those bags. It also beeps for 98 of the 998 bags that hold nothing banned.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a test result into a probability by counting people, and see why a rare condition makes most positives wrong.

recap.keyIdea: The chance that a positive result is right is true positives divided by all positives. When the condition is rare, false positives swamp the true ones, so ignoring the base rate misleads.

blocks.text: You counted 9 true positives against 99 false positives, so a positive meant 8.3%, not 90%. In the clinic at 10% prevalence the same test gave 50%, and the witness who named blue was right only 42.9% of the time.

recap.nextHook: Counting people fixes this error. Other errors come from the first number we meet, true or not.

questions.prompt: 2,000 people are tested for a condition that 5% have. The test detects 80% of cases and gives false positives for 10% of people without it. How many people test positive in total?
hints: 5% of 2,000 have the condition.
Find the true positives and the false positives separately.
Add the two groups of positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 have it, 80 test positive; 1,900 do not, 190 test positive; 80 + 190 = 270.

questions.onCorrect: Add the true positives and the false positives: the flagged group is everyone with a positive result.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the true positives. Add the false positives too.
That counts only the false positives. Add the true positives too.

questions.prompt: A doctor judges a positive result from a 90%-accurate test as 90% likely to be right, ignoring that the disease is rare. What is this error called?
hints: The neglected number is how common the condition is to begin with.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Base-rate neglect: the prior frequency of the condition is ignored.

questions.onCorrect: Ignoring how rare a condition is when judging a result is base-rate neglect.

misconceptions.feedback: Confirmation bias favours evidence that fits what you believe. This error ignores how common the condition is.

questions.prompt: Of 1,000 people, 5% have a condition. The test flags 80% of cases and 10% of people without it. What percentage of positive results are correct? Give one decimal place.
hints: Count the people with and without the condition.
Find the true positives and the false positives separately.
Divide the true positives by all positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 have it and 40 test positive; 950 do not and 95 test positive. 40 ÷ 135 = 0.296, or 29.6%.

questions.onCorrect: True positives over all positives: even a good test is wrong most of the time when the condition is rare.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hit rate. The question asks what share of positives are right.
That is the number of true positives. Turn it into a share of all positives.

questions.prompt: A bag beeps. Roughly how likely is it that it holds the banned item?
hints: Count how many bags beep in total.
Of all the bags that beep, how many hold the banned item?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 2 in 100: 2 true beeps among 100 bags that beep.

questions.onCorrect: Counting the beeps shows that most are false alarms. You used natural frequencies without being told.

misconceptions.feedback: Count how many bags beep and how many of those are real.
That is the scanner's success rate on bags that hold the item, not the chance that a beeping bag does.

questions.prompt: Of 500 people, 4% have a condition. How many people is that?
hints: A percentage of a group is a number of people.
Find 1% of 500 first.
Multiply that by 4.
questions.onCorrect: Work with people, not percentages: 4% of 500 is 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage. Apply it to the 500 people.
That takes 20% of the group. Use the percentage given.

questions.prompt: How many false positives are there?
hints: First find how many people do not have the disease.
Subtract the 1% who have it from 1,000.
Take 10% of that number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000 − 10 = 990 people do not have the disease; 10% of 990 = 99 false positives.

questions.onCorrect: False positives come only from people without the disease, a much bigger group than those who have it.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the error rate of the wrong group. False positives come from people who do not have the disease.
That takes the error rate of everyone. False positives come only from those who do not have the disease.

questions.prompt: A screening finds 4 true positives and 16 false positives. What percentage of the positive results are correct?
hints: The flagged group is the true positives plus the false positives.
Add 4 and 16.
Divide the true positives by that total.
questions.onCorrect: Divide true positives by all positives: here one in five positives is right.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the false positives alone. Divide by everyone flagged.
That is the share of positives that are wrong.

questions.prompt: Why divide by all 120 positives, not by the 50 people who have the disease?
hints: Who is the question about: everyone, or someone who tested positive?

acceptedIdeas: The person tested positive, so they are one of the 120 people flagged.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The question is about someone who tested positive, so the flagged group is the whole of the comparison.

choices.label: Because the 50 people do not count.
The person tested positive, so they are one of the 120 people flagged.

questions.onCorrect: The person has tested positive, so they are one of the flagged. That group is the denominator.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide the denominator. The question does.
The 50 are counted, as the true positives among the flagged.

questions.prompt: What is the probability, as a percentage, that a person who tests positive has the disease? Give one decimal place.
hints: Restrict attention to people who tested positive.
The true positives are the people in that group who have the disease.
Divide 9 by the total number of positives and round.
questions.onCorrect: True positives over all positives, not the test's hit rate: most positives here are false alarms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the test's hit rate. The question asks how many positives are right.
That is the number of true positives. Turn it into a share of all positives.
That divides by the false positives alone. Divide by everyone flagged.

questions.prompt: What percentage of positive results are true positives?
hints: Count the people with and without the disease first.
Apply 90% to the first group and 10% to the second.
Divide true positives by all positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 have it and 90 test positive; 900 do not and 90 test positive; 90/180 = 50%.

questions.onCorrect: The same test, a different base rate: true positives now equal false positives, so a positive is a coin toss.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hit rate. The question asks what share of positives are true.
That is the share who have the disease. Ask how many positives are true.

questions.prompt: 20% of a city's cabs are blue. A witness who names colours correctly 75% of the time says the cab was blue. What is the probability, as a percentage, that it was blue? Give one decimal place.
hints: Imagine 1,000 cabs: 200 blue and 800 green.
The witness calls 75% of blue cabs blue and 25% of green cabs blue.
Divide correct 'blue' calls by all 'blue' calls.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Per 1,000 cabs: 150 blue cabs called blue and 200 green cabs called blue; 150/350 = 42.9%.

questions.onCorrect: Count the cabs the witness calls blue: true calls over all calls. The many green cabs produce many wrong calls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the witness's accuracy, not the chance that this cab was blue.
That is the base rate alone. The witness's report adds evidence.
That is the share of 'blue' calls that were wrong.

citations.claim: Natural frequencies turn percentages into counts of people, which makes a test result easy to read. Picture 1,000 people. If 2% have a condition, that is 20 people. If a test catches half of them, that is 10 true positives. Counting people avoids multiplying percentages in your head. A percentage of a group is a number of people. Work with the number.

1,000 people are screened for a disease that 1% have. The test flags 90% of those who have it, so there are 9 true positives. It also wrongly flags 10% of people who do not have the disease. False positives outnumber the true positives by more than ten to one. The healthy group is large, so even a small error rate flags many people.

The chance that a positive result is right is the true positives divided by all positives. A positive result puts you among everyone the test flagged: the true positives plus the false positives. Most people answer near the test's hit rate instead. Ignoring how rare the condition is, is base-rate neglect. Ask who is in the flagged group, and how many of them have the condition.

500 people are tested; 10% have the disease. The test flags 60% of cases and 20% of healthy people. What share of positives are right? Split the people into those with and without the disease. 10% of 500 = 50, so 450 do not Count the true positives and the false positives. 60% of 50 = 30 and 20% of 450 = 90 Divide the true positives by all positives. 30 ÷ (30 + 90) = 30 ÷ 120 = 25%

Of 1,000 people, 9 true positives and 99 false positives test positive. A person is among the flagged. Only 9 of the 108 flagged people have the disease. Answering with the test's 90% hit rate would be badly wrong.

Use the same test, with a 90% hit rate and a 10% false-alarm rate, in a clinic where 10% of 1,000 people have the disease. Nothing about the test changed, yet a positive now means far more. The meaning of a result depends on who is being tested.

In a city, 20% of cabs are blue and the rest green. A witness names colours correctly 75% of the time. Picture 1,000 cabs: 200 blue and 800 green. A witness who names colours reliably is still more likely wrong than right here, because green cabs are so much more common.

2,000 people are tested for a condition that 5% have. The test detects 80% of cases and gives false positives for 10% of people without it. How many people test positive in total? 100 have it, 80 test positive; 1,900 do not, 190 test positive; 80 + 190 = 270.

A doctor judges a positive result from a 90%-accurate test as 90% likely to be right, ignoring that the disease is rare. What is this error called? Base-rate neglect: the prior frequency of the condition is ignored.

Of 1,000 people, 5% have a condition. The test flags 80% of cases and 10% of people without it. What percentage of positive results are correct? Give one decimal place. 50 have it and 40 test positive; 950 do not and 95 test positive. 40 ÷ 135 = 0.296, or 29.6%.
A bag beeps. Roughly how likely is it that it holds the banned item? About 2 in 100: 2 true beeps among 100 bags that beep.
Of 500 people, 4% have a condition. How many people is that? 4% of 500 = 20 people.
How many false positives are there? 1,000 − 10 = 990 people do not have the disease; 10% of 990 = 99 false positives.
A screening finds 4 true positives and 16 false positives. What percentage of the positive results are correct? 4 ÷ (4 + 16) = 4 ÷ 20 = 20%.
Why divide by all 120 positives, not by the 50 people who have the disease? The question is about someone who tested positive, so the flagged group is the whole of the comparison.
What is the probability, as a percentage, that a person who tests positive has the disease? Give one decimal place. 9/(9 + 99) = 9/108 = 0.0833, or 8.3%.
What percentage of positive results are true positives? 100 have it and 90 test positive; 900 do not and 90 test positive; 90/180 = 50%.

20% of a city's cabs are blue. A witness who names colours correctly 75% of the time says the cab was blue. What is the probability, as a percentage, that it was blue? Give one decimal place. Per 1,000 cabs: 150 blue cabs called blue and 200 green cabs called blue; 150/350 = 42.9%.

1,000 people are screened for a condition that 2% have. The test misses no cases but gives false positives for 5% of people without it. How many false positives are there? 980 do not have it; 5% of 980 = 49.
A screening programme finds 12 true positives and 36 false positives. What percentage of positive results are correct? 12/(12 + 36) = 12/48 = 25%.
